items.question: What does brain imaging show about brain activity?
options: Every region does something across a day
Roughly a tenth of it ever switches on
One hemisphere runs while the other rests
Activity stops in areas you rarely use
items.explanation: Different jobs light up different areas minute to minute, and over a day the whole thing gets used — though never every cell at once, which would be a seizure. The ten percent line was never a research finding.

items.question: Which body parts get the biggest share of your brain's movement map?
items.explanation: Brain space is handed out by how finely a part has to be controlled, not by how big it is. Your thigh is enormous and gets a sliver; your lips and fingertips get a wide stretch of cortex.

items.question: Which side of your brain does most of the steering when you move your right hand?
items.explanation: Most movement nerves cross over on their way down, so each half of the brain mainly runs the opposite half of the body. Nobody is certain why the wiring crosses, but it does in nearly every animal with a backbone.

items.question: Why is it so hard to tickle yourself?
options: Your fingers go numb when you try
Tickle nerves switch off in your hands
You cannot reach the ticklish spots
Your brain predicts your own touch
items.explanation: Your brain sends a copy of every movement order over to the touch areas, so the sensation arrives already expected and gets turned down. Surprise is most of what tickling is.

items.question: Why is patting your head while rubbing your stomach tricky?
options: Your arms share one nerve to the brain
The two rhythms pull toward each other
The brain can plan only one arm at a time
Circles take longer than pats to learn
items.explanation: Two different patterns running at once tend to blend, and both hands drift toward doing the same thing. People who get it usually slow right down and let each hand start on its own.

items.question: When you lift one arm quickly, which muscles fire first?
items.explanation: Your body braces before it moves, because swinging an arm up would otherwise tip you forward. The bracing happens a fraction of a second early and you never notice ordering it.

items.question: What happens to most people's walking while they do hard mental math?
options: It slows and gets less even
It speeds up without them noticing
items.explanation: Walking looks automatic but still borrows attention, and a demanding thought takes some of it back. Researchers use that slow-down as a way to measure how automatic someone's walking has become.

items.question: What happens when you return to a skill you learned years ago and dropped?
options: It has to be learned again from zero
It comes back quicker than before
It returns only with a coach's help
It feels new for about the same time
items.explanation: The pattern was never erased, only left alone, so practice is rebuilding instead of building. Riding a bike is the famous case, but it holds for swimming strokes and instruments too.

items.question: Do people react faster to a sound or to a flash of light?
options: To the light, by a lot
items.explanation: Sound reaches the parts of the brain that trigger a movement through a shorter chain than vision does. The gap is only a few hundredths of a second, which is part of why sprint races start with a gun and not a lamp.

items.question: What do your movement areas do while you watch someone else move?
options: They shut down while you watch
They wait until it is your turn
They quietly light up as well
They run the motion in your muscles
items.explanation: Watching a movement partly rehearses it, which is part of why showing teaches faster than telling. It is not the same as doing it — the final order to actually contract gets held back.

items.question: Which part of your tongue picks up sweet tastes?
options: Every part that has taste buds
Only the tip at the front
The middle, where it is smooth
items.explanation: The taste map in old textbooks came from a chart of small differences in sensitivity that got redrawn as separate zones. Every taste-bud region answers to all the basic tastes, including the roof of your mouth.

items.question: Which of these is a real sense your body has, beyond the famous five?
options: A sense of your own balance
A sense of the time of year
items.explanation: The five-senses list comes from ancient philosophy rather than biology. Balance has its own organ in the inner ear, and temperature and limb position are separate systems again — researchers disagree about where the list should end.

items.question: Why does your recorded voice sound wrong to you?
options: Microphones cut the lowest notes out
You hear your voice a beat delayed
You normally hear it through bone too
Recordings raise every pitch a little
items.explanation: Speaking sends sound to your ears two ways, through the air and through the bones of your skull, and the bone path adds a depth the recording never had. Everybody else has only ever heard the air version.

items.question: Why does food taste flat when your nose is blocked?
options: A blocked nose dries the tongue
Much of flavor is really smell
The tongue cools and slows down
items.explanation: Your tongue reports only a handful of basics — sweet, salty, sour, bitter, savory. Everything that makes strawberry taste like strawberry travels up the back of your nose while you chew.

items.question: What is true about catching a yawn from somebody?
options: People stop catching them by ten
items.explanation: Catching yawns tends to appear around age four or five rather than at birth, and dogs will yawn back at a person they know well. Why yawns exist at all is still being argued over.

items.question: What happens to what you see during a blink?
options: You see a brief flash of gray
Your eyes keep a faint image
items.explanation: Vision gets dialed down just before the lid moves and picked back up after, so the darkness never reaches awareness. The same trick hides the blur every time your eyes jump from word to word.

items.question: What is a person's normal body temperature?
options: A peak right after waking up
A figure that swings all day
items.explanation: Readings run lower in the early morning and higher in the late afternoon, and healthy people differ from one another. The famous single figure was an average taken in the 1800s.

items.question: Where does digestion actually begin?
items.explanation: Saliva carries an enzyme that starts breaking starch apart before you swallow. Hold a plain cracker on your tongue without chewing and you can taste it turn sweet.

items.question: What job do your eyebrows do besides showing how you feel?
items.explanation: The hairs run sideways, out toward your temples, so anything running down your forehead gets sent around your eyes instead of into them. Eyelashes are the ones that handle dust.

items.question: Why do your eyes water when somebody cuts an onion?
options: A gas from the onion stings
items.explanation: Cutting breaks open cells that had been keeping two chemicals apart, and what they make drifts up as a gas that irritates the surface of the eye. Chilling the onion first slows the reaction down.

items.question: How does a newborn's number of bones compare with an adult's?
items.explanation: Many bones start out as separate pieces with cartilage between them and knit together through childhood — the skull and the hip bones both do it. The soft spots on a baby's head are that process still unfinished.

items.question: Which bone in your body connects to no other bone?
items.explanation: The hyoid is a small U-shaped bone in the neck, held in place by muscles and ligaments alone. It anchors your tongue and the muscles you swallow with.

items.question: What shape does a healthy spine make from the side?
items.explanation: The curves work like a spring, spreading the load of your head and letting the column flex. A perfectly straight stack would pass the shock of every step straight up to your skull.

items.question: What moves food along inside you after you swallow?
options: The same muscle as your arms
items.explanation: The tube has its own muscle layers that squeeze in waves, working whether or not you think about them. It is why astronauts can swallow perfectly well with no gravity to help.

items.question: Why does your elbow need a muscle on each side?
options: One side works, one side rests
Each side handles half the weight
Muscles can pull but not push
Bone would snap under one muscle
items.explanation: A muscle shortens; that is its only move. Bending takes one muscle pulling, and straightening takes a different one on the opposite side pulling the other way.

items.question: What is different about the muscle fibers used for sprinting?
options: They are longer than the others
They sit closer to the skin
They contract fast and tire fast
items.explanation: Everyone carries a mix of quick-tiring and slow-tiring fibers inside the same muscle, and which ones get called on depends on how hard and how fast the job is. The proportions differ from person to person.

items.question: Which of these can rebuild itself after it is damaged?
items.explanation: Bone is living tissue with its own blood supply, so cells knit a break back together. Enamel was built by cells that die off once the tooth is finished, leaving nothing behind to do repairs.

items.question: Where does the warmth come from when you start moving?
items.explanation: Muscles are not tidy machines — a good share of the energy they use leaves as heat instead of movement. Shivering is your body putting that same inefficiency to work on purpose.

items.question: What is unusual about your lowest pair of ribs?
items.explanation: Most ribs curve around and join the breastbone through cartilage, but the bottom pair simply ends in the muscle of your side. They are called floating ribs, and they are part of why your lower trunk twists more easily than your chest.

items.question: Why can your eyes aim more precisely than your legs can?
items.explanation: A nerve cell and the muscle fibers it controls fire together as one unit, so the fewer fibers per nerve, the finer the adjustment possible. Eye muscles run a handful each; a big leg muscle can run many hundreds at once.
